Why the Quran Says We, He, and I

The Quran's We is the Arabic plural of majesty, its He is the same Speaker presenting Himself, and its I is that Speaker at His nearest, shown from the grammarians, the poets, the book's own usage, the school's tafsir, the hadith of the Ahl al-Bayt, and the opponent's own canon.
The Argument Under Examination

The charge comes in two forms, and both travel widely. The first asks it as arithmetic. Your book says We created you, We sent down the Reminder, We built the heaven. A plural speaker is plural, so who are the others helping Allah? The second asks it as confusion. The same book keeps moving between We, He, and I, sometimes inside one passage, and a speaker who knows who he is does not keep changing his own pronouns.

Both forms assume one thing, that an Arabic pronoun counts its referents the way an English pronoun does. It does not. Arabic has a standing plural of majesty, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books, alive in the poets, and used by the Quran itself for single referents of no theological weight at all. When the Quran means that others act alongside Allah, it names them. When it wants the nearness of answer, it drops the say-command and speaks as I. When it describes the Lord for the servant to learn of Him, it says He. One Speaker, and many rooms of speech.
Conclusion

The We carries majesty and never number, and no helper hides inside it, because the plural of majesty is ordinary Arabic and the Quran names its co-agents when it has them. The shifts of person follow design, because iltifat is a named device the Imams themselves use. The charge survives only by reading an Arabic pronoun as an English census, and that method convicts Genesis before it reaches the sura of the Reminder.
The Facts
Islamic dates are AH; dates for Christian figures and councils are CE.
1. The Grammar and the Lexicon

The case here is addressed to any reader who accepts Arabic dictionaries, grammar, and poetry as evidence. The charge rests on one grammatical assumption, that a pronoun counts its referents. Arabic breaks that assumption before the Quran is even opened. The language has a plural of majesty, nahnu, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books with the Quran's own We as the textbook example.

Contested words. The charge reads nahnu, the Arabic we, as a count of speakers, and the person-shifts as a change of speaker. The grammarians, the lexicon's witnesses, the poets, and the Quran's own usage fix nahnu as register, and the shifts as a named device with named purposes.

The school's senior classical commentator states the rule first. The speech of one speaker can run in the plural form for greatness of station, and he says this is simply how speakers of Arabic talk. His proof text is the charge's own target, the doubled We of the Reminder verse (Qur'an 15:9), and the We of man's creation (Qur'an 23:12). The report he relays records both edges. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, a founder of Arabic grammar, was asked about the plural of the dying soul's plea in Qur'an 23:99, send them back, addressed to the one God. He declined to force a parse and said he does not know its analysis, because it is a plural, and the people of his circle found the reserve good. The reserve predates the rule, and the rule answers the reserve. The founder's own stated reason is form-side, because it is a plural, and the Kufan school answered him within a generation. That reading is exhibited below. Al-Tusi's statement is the tradition resolving what the founder left open, the plural of rank named where he paused. It runs in both directions, a creature addressing the one God in the plural and God speaking of Himself in it. Neither direction carries number.
Source: al-Tusi (d.460), al-Tibyan, v7, p394
Speaker: al-Tusi, relaying al-Nadr ibn Sumayl from al-Khalil
Claim: the speech of the One runs in the plural form for greatness of station, as speakers of Arabic say
Locus: Qur'an 23:99 with 15:9 and 23:12 as parallels
The grammar of the Quran reaches the same verdict in the same breath, and it answers the angels reading by name.
Source: al-'Ukbari (d.616), al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an, p274
Claim: the plural of Qur'an 23:99 is a plural of magnification, with the angels reading stated among three alternatives
Locus: Qur'an 15:9, and 6:99's one sentence under two persons, Allah sent down and We brought forth, with no second agent between them

The Founding School Reads It Plainly. The grammar books cited so far were written in the fifth century and after. The rule they state is older than their ink, and the earliest layer of the record shows it.
Source: al-Farra (d.207), Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v3, p42
Speaker: al-Farra, the Kufan school's founding layer
Claim: the Arabs use the plural verb for one person, and the Quran itself does it, addressing the single Prophet in the plural
Locus: Qur'an 44:36 with 65:1 and 23:99 as parallels

Al-Farra, who died in 207 and took the Kufan school from the generation of al-Kisa'i, the Kufan master reader of the Quran, is commenting on Qur'an 44:36. There the opponents address the Prophet ﷺ alone. He says the plural verb for the one addressee is ordinary Arabic, and his parallel is inside the Quran itself. The sura of divorce opens, O Prophet, when you divorce, with the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause (Qur'an 65:1). The dying soul's send me back (Qur'an 23:99) is, he says, of the same kind. The later tafsir commonly reads the plural of 65:1 as a turn to the community with the Prophet; al-Farra's reading is the Kufan school's, and the exhibit claims no consensus. The book itself addresses one man in the plural and reports one man addressing his one Lord in the plural.
The same grammarian equates the divine Our with the creature's plural in one breath.
Source: al-Farra (d.207), Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p13
Claim: the divine Our of the ark is plural in form and singular in meaning, parsed like the creature's plural of 23:99
Locus: Qur'an 11:37 with 23:99 and 11:27

The ark built under Our eyes and by Our revelation (Qur'an 11:37) is, on al-Farra's gloss, plural in form and singular in meaning, parsed exactly like send me back. And the comparison behind his gloss runs the same way. His earlier reading of rather we think you liars (Qur'an 11:27) took the plural you as addressed to Noah alone, one man receiving the plural of address. The divine We and the creature's exalted plural are one fact of the language to the founding school, not two problems. And he says so while holding the dying soul's verse in view.
Source: al-Farra (d.207), Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p241, the sentence continues below
Claim: the dying soul's plural runs on the same usage as the divine We created you
Locus: Qur'an 23:99 with 19:9, across a page boundary
Source: al-Farra (d.207), Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p242, the continuation
Claim: the same usage covers what Allah says of Himself, We created you before

The verse runs its verb as though for a plurality, though the dying man called upon his Lord alone. This, al-Farra says, runs on the same usage as what Allah says of Himself, We created you before (Qur'an 19:9, in his cited reading, where the transmitted text has I created you). The Kufan school had printed the rule with the Quran's own verses generations before the fifth-century glosses, inside the school that grew up around the book's own recitation.

Back in the dictionary of Ibn Manzur, the lexicon's own witnesses carry the same usage at every register of speech. They carry it in the lexicon itself, the class of evidence the contested word demands.
Source: Ibn Manzur (d.711), Lisan al-'Arab, v6, p229, root n-d-s
Claim: three rank-we witnesses at three registers, the raid poet, the tribal house, and the Prophet's company of prophets, each a we of rank, none a bare count of doers

The Shia school states the same rule where its own heart is, the wilaya verse. Qur'an 5:55 describes one man, Ali ﵇, who gave zakat in the moment of bowing. The verse says they establish the prayer and they pay the zakat, a plural in form with one referent in fact. The school's case for the Imam's designation stands on this grammar.
Source: Abu al-Salah al-Halabi (d.447), Taqrib al-Ma'arif, p188
Claim: expressing the one by the plural of magnification is manifest Arabic, stated in defense of 5:55
Abu Ali relays al-Zamakhshari's gloss on 5:55 and then goes past it. The school does not borrow the conclusion from the Sunni philologist. It states the rule to him.
Source: Abu Ali, in Ma'rifa al-Imam, v5, p24
Speaker: Abu Ali, relaying al-Zamakhshari (d.538) on Qur'an 5:55
Claim: the plural form for one referent is too famous in the language to need proof
And the modern school commentary applies the same rule to the divine We itself, beside the plural for the Imam.
Source: al-Mar'ashi (d.1411), Sharh Ihqaq al-Haqq, v3, p587
Claim: the one is expressed by the plural of magnification in Qur'an 97:1 as in 5:55
The grammar is settled, and the lexicon carries it. Whether the living usage agrees is the next question, and the poets answer it.
2. How the Kings and Poets Said We

Every human we on exhibit gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people, and the divine We gathers rank without needing any. The case of a speaker standing alone rests on three legs. The grammar of section 1 states the rule. The kings' custom, which al-Razi explains in section 7, shows it in use. And the verse of the two directions, Qur'an 23:99, has a creature addressing the one God in the plural inside the book itself. The grammarians wrote after the book, and the book is their largest text. The poets and the kings' custom are the usage no scripture controls. And the question of codification cuts both ways. A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else. This rule explains the poets, the kings, the dying soul's plea, and the book at once, and a rule that explains all of them was already in the language. The demand for a pre-Islamic king saying we of himself alone should also be measured against the opponent's own ground. The only divine plurals his canon carries are in-scripture, Genesis 1:26 and its companions, and the only in-scripture plural-for-one the Quran needs is likewise inside the book, the dying soul's plea and the single Prophet addressed in the plural. A bar that the opponent's own evidence does not clear is not a bar the Quran has to clear.
Source: Nashwan al-Himyari (d.573), Shams al-'Ulum, v3, p287
Speaker: Imru' al-Qays, the Jāhiliyya's most famous poet
Claim: the royal we in the poets' mouth, rank without census

No reader counts the speakers of that line. The line ranks them. And the same art allows a speaker to present himself in the third person when grandeur calls for it, which is the register the Quran enters when it says He of Allah.
Source: al-Razi (d.606), Tafsir al-Razi, v6, p216
Speaker: al-Hutay'a, asked to name the greatest poet
Claim: the poet names himself the third, and the grandeur survives because he did not say myself
The rhetoricians gave the whole device a name and a taxonomy, and they found their textbook example in the same poet.
Source: al-Sharif al-Jurjani (d.816), al-Hashiya 'ala al-Kashshaf, p63
Claim: iltifat is a classified device of Arabic eloquence, with Imru' al-Qays's your-night as a textbook case

The usage is alive and the device has a name. The poets practiced the shifts long before the Quran, and the rhetoricians came later and named what the poets had been doing. Whether the Quran itself keeps this bookkeeping is the next question, and the book answers on its own terms.
3. The Same Act in Two Pronouns

The strongest test of a reading is the book that provoked it. If the We of the Quran counted speakers, the Quran would use its plurals only where referents are many. It does the opposite, and a Shia scholar of the sixth century drew up the evidence.
Source: Ibn Shahrashub (d.588), Mutashabih al-Qur'an, v2, p272
Claim: a catalogue of the Quran's plural forms with single referents, the mosques that is one mosque, the callers that are one caller, the dual addressed to two

A book that says the mosques for one mosque cannot be heard to count speakers in its pronouns. The catalogue proves the point for plural forms in the third person. The first person is fixed by the grammarians of section 1 and the kings' custom of section 2, and together the two close both doors, the form and the person. The book also describes the same act with both pronouns, and the school's own literature moves between them without effort.
Source: Manaqib Ibn Shahrashub, relayed in Bihar al-Anwar, v16, p336
Claim: one narration proving the Prophet's beauty cites the He of 82:7 and the We of 95:4 side by side
Verse: Qur'an 82:7 and Qur'an 95:4
Claim: man's creation in He and the same creation in We

Creation in He. Creation in We. One act, one God, two registers, and the commentators who cite the two verses together sense no change of actor between them. And the same family of pairs runs through the breath of the spirit itself, into the verse nearest the opponent's own theology.
Verse: Qur'an 38:71-72 and Qur'an 66:12
Claim: one kind of act, the breath of the spirit, carried in He and I at Adam and in We at Jesus

The Lord said, the third person of relay. I am creating, and I breathed of My spirit, the first person of the giving, in Adam's making, with the same wording at Qur'an 15:29. And We breathed of Our spirit, the plural of majesty, in the making of Jesus within Mary. The Christian reader meets the We at the verse nearest his own theology, and the person it carries there is the same One who said I at Adam.

Where helpers exist, the book names them. The charge asks whether anyone helps Allah, and the book answers by grammar. When creatures share in an act, the Quran never hides them in a pronoun. It names them, coordinates them, and puts them under permission.
Verse: Qur'an 2:34
Claim: the angels are the addressees of We said, never the co-speakers
Verse: Qur'an 33:56
Claim: when Allah and the angels share one verb, the verse names both parties in coordination
Verse: Qur'an 19:64
Claim: the angels' own we, marked by their Lord's command, is the discriminant of the book's speakers

The verse of Allah and His angels under one verb has its own page on this site, the page on whether Allah prays, answered from the same grammar. Here it carries one point, that shared action is named action.
Verse: Qur'an 6:99, opening clause
Claim: one sentence, two persons, one subject, He sent down and We brought forth, with no second agent between them

There is the one-sentence shift itself, exhibited. He sent down, then We brought forth, inside a single clause chain, the subject unchanged and no agent entering between them. Different hands cannot hide inside one sentence, and the book puts its person-shift exactly there.

In Qur'an 19:64 the we is the angels' own voice, the Prophet the addressee, and their Lord named in the third person with His command as their only warrant. The verse proves the telling difference. When the we is the angels', the book puts it in the angels' mouth and marks it by their Lord's command. The one sentence of Qur'an 6:99 shows the other pole, where Allah sent down and We brought forth under one subject. When the we is Allah's, it stands alone and unmarked. Where the mufassirun, the Quran commentators, have heard the angels sharing in an act, they pointed to the verses that name them. Those verses are the descent by permission (Qur'an 97:4) and the wings (Qur'an 35:1). The plural of majesty is never left carrying them unmarked. The naming rule is the book's own way of telling its speakers apart, and this verse is its proof text.
Verse: Qur'an 97:1-4
Claim: the Night of Decree does both in one sura, the We of the descent and the angels' own verb under permission
Verse: Qur'an 50:16
Claim: nearness itself is said in the We here and in the I of Qur'an 2:186, one nearness, two registers
Verse: Qur'an 15:9
Claim: the doubled We of the Reminder verse, whose carriers are named elsewhere, Jibril upon the heart by Allah's permission (Qur'an 2:97) and the Trustworthy Spirit (Qur'an 26:193)

The sending is one. The We is Allah's. The carriers are named elsewhere, which is exactly where the book wants them. The book's bookkeeping forbids reading number into its pronouns, and the remaining question is where the We sits doctrinally.
4. Where the We Meets the One God

If the We carried any scent of partnership, the book would keep it away from its oneness passages. It does the opposite. The We-soaked run of al-Dhariyat closes on the first person and the ban on another god.
Verse: Qur'an 51:47-51
Claim: We built, We spread, We created pairs, then flee to Allah, I am a warner, and do not set up with Allah another god

One passage, three persons, and the We lives next door to the first person and to the book's ban on partners. The school's commentators read the passage exactly so, and the gloss on the pairs runs to the section's point, the oneness of the Creator of every pair.
Source: al-Tabrisi (d.548), Majma' al-Bayan, v9, p267
Claim: the We-verses are read with the tawhid they serve, power without need
Source: al-Tabrisi, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p329
Claim: the pairs of creation are given so you may know that the Creator of these pairs is One, whom nothing resembles
Source: al-Tabataba'i (d.1402), al-Mizan, v18, p381
Claim: the verses are marshaled to establish His oneness in lordship, concluding in the flight to Allah

The sura of pure oneness answers in the He, the register of the Lord being taught, and its occasion of revelation was a question about lineage. The Jews asked the Prophet what his Lord's lineage was, and the answer was the sura of the One. The gloss transmitted in the school's earliest tafsir closes the helpers question with five denials.
Source: Tafsir al-Qummi (d.329), v2, p448
Dating: the Jews asked the Prophet the Lord's lineage
Claim: no equal, no likeness, no partner, no backer, no helper

The sura that says He is the sura that denies every companion the charge hopes to find inside We. The We is majesty inside a book that banks its oneness beside it. The confusion half of the charge remains, the question of who speaks when the book says He, and the school's answer has three parts, a named device, a named relay, and a named occasion.
5. The Person-Shifts Have a Name

The scholarly form of the charge reads person-shifts as the seams of different authors. The exhibits answer it before the device is even named. The shifts sit inside single sentences (Qur'an 6:99) and single passages (Qur'an 51:47-51), where different hands cannot hide, and the same act carries both pronouns (Qur'an 82:7 and 95:4). The device itself the rhetoricians named, and the school's commentary assigns its purposes verse by verse.
Source: al-Mashhadi (d.1125), Kanz al-Daqa'iq, v1, p118
Claim: the Fatiha's shift to You exchanges the obscurity of absence for the clarity of presence
Source: al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, v3, p377
Claim: the verses carry shifts of address and of overt noun for pronoun, with purposes clear to the reflecting reader
Source: al-Mazandarani (d.1081), Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v1, p122
Claim: Qur'an 2:168's shift from address to absence marks the hearers' distance from the rank of address
One grammar serves the book and the house. The Imams use the device the Quran uses, which settles what kind of device it is.
Source: al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v3, p204
Claim: Imam al-Rida's we is a shift from third person to first for stating the object openly, like Ali naming himself Haydara
The Sunni rhetorical tradition reaches the same verdict on the same terms, on a verse whose base form is first person and whose shift to the naming of Allah is the art.
Source: al-Iskandari (d.683), al-Insaf, v2, p174
Claim: the shift of Qur'an 9:2 is virtuosity in the methods of eloquence, magnifying the station and the matter
Verse: Qur'an 2:97
Claim: the carrier named, Jibril, who brings it down upon the Prophet's heart by Allah's permission

There is the say-verse grammar in one exhibit. The verse opens with say, Allah composing the Prophet's exact words, and inside the composed words the carrier is named, Jibril, and the permission is named, by Allah's permission. The relay is not an inference. The book prints it.

When the book says He, Allah speaks, and the carriers are named. The clearest statement is the gloss on 69:40, the word of a noble messenger, and it is Allah's speech placed on his tongue. Add the grammar of the say-verses, where Allah composes the Prophet's exact words, and the architecture is complete. Allah speaks, Jibril carries to the Prophet's heart, the Prophet recites, and each layer is grammatically visible in the book. Third-person self-presentation plus named relay is the book's standing design. One shift has a recorded occasion, and it prepares the last section. A questioner asked the Prophet whether the Lord is near, that they should whisper, or far, that they should call out. The answer came down without the say-command, and the Lord answered the questioner in His own person.
Source: al-Tabrisi's gloss, relayed in Bihar al-Anwar, v18, p173
Claim: the Quran is the word of a noble messenger, Jibril, and it is Allah's speech sent down upon his tongue
Source: from al-Hasan, in Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v1, p118
Dating: is our Lord near that we whisper, or far that we call out
Claim: the I-verse came down answering the questioner directly
The shifts are design, the relay is named, and the occasion of the I is recorded. What the answering I sounds like in the school's own transmission is the next room.
6. Allah Answers in His Own I

The reports of the Ahl al-Bayt do not debate the pronouns. They pray with them, counsel with them, and narrate Allah answering in them. A Christian reader weighs these chains as the school's testimony, and sections 1 through 4 carry the case on ground he already accepts.
Verse: Qur'an 2:186
Claim: the I of nearness and answer, with the relay command dropped

The verse is spoken to the Prophet, when My servants ask you about Me, so the relay stands inside the sentence. What drops is the say-command that stands before most answers, so the answer itself comes in Allah's own person, I am near, with no commanded recitation between. The narration that holds all three persons in one report enacts the very turn al-Mashhadi explained, the described Lord becoming the answering One.
Source: al-Saduq (d.381), 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, v1, p269
Chain: through the twelve Imams from Ali from the Prophet from Allah
Claim: at every verse of the Fatiha Allah answers the servant in His own first person

The answering I is also the school's liturgy. The glorification of the hours strings the first person declaration by declaration, and the Imam teaches it as the servant's own supplication, with the promise that the need of whoever calls with it is granted.
Source: Imam al-Sadiq, in al-Kafi, v2, p515
Claim: the glorification of the hours strings first-person declarations of Allah, taught as the servant's supplication
And the liturgy counsels. A companion whose hope was weakening after years of waiting heard the I-verse read to him as a promise to stand on.
Source: Abu al-Hasan, in al-Kafi, v2, p489
Claim: the Imam meets a weakening heart with the I-verse itself, a promise to stand on
The Night of Decree layers the persons inside one report, the sura's We, the third person of the permission, and then the Lord's own gloss in the first person.
Source: Imam al-Sadiq, relaying Ali ibn al-Husayn, in al-Kafi, v1, p296
Claim: the Night of Decree layers We, He, and My in one report, ending in My angels and My spirit saluting the Prophet with My peace
The consolation hadith joins the We-verse to the I-revelation directly, one Speaker at two registers in the space of two sentences.
Source: Imam al-Kazim, in al-Kafi, v1, p474
Claim: the We-verse of the angels' prostration is followed by Allah's first-person consolation of the Prophet
The riwa'i, the transmitted reports of the school, treat the pronouns as address. What the rest of the tradition says is the last question, and it agrees.
7. The Sunni Mufassirun Say the Same

The strongest corroboration is a mufassir the polemic's own audience reveres, the same al-Razi already met explaining the poet's third, answering the polemic's own question eight centuries before it was asked.
Source: al-Razi (d.606), Tafsir al-Razi, v28, p225
Claim: the We built it is more decisive against a partner than I built it, and the register is the king's we

The king says we did, meaning that his servants did it at his command, and there is magnification in it. The obvious objection belongs here, beside the quote. If the king's we means his servants, does Allah's We mean His angels? The naming rule of section 3 answers. Wherever creatures act, the book names them, and named creatures under command are the retinue, worshippers who descend by permission, not helpers sharing the act's rank. The custom explains the register. The naming rule polices the referents. The verdict is not al-Razi's alone.
Source: Abu Hayyan (d.745), al-Bahr al-Muhit, v7, p346
Claim: the plural of 37:75 is for greatness and majesty
Al-Alusi states the same verdict on the same verse, and adds the report of the Prophet's own prayer at it.
Source: al-Alusi (d.1270), Ruh al-Ma'ani, v12, p96
Claim: the same verdict on 37:75, with the Prophet's own prayer at the plural-of-majesty verse
Source: al-Sha'rawi (d.1419), Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, v5, p232
Claim: the I points to the oneness of the Essence and the We to the gathering of the attributes of perfection, the grammarians' rule that the plural pronouns belong to the one magnifying himself

And the register itself answers the Trinity's form of plurality. Attributes gathered in one essence are what the One has. Persons are who the One is. The Quran's We gathers the first and never divides the second. The frame is register, and register does not count. Lexicon, usage, the book's bookkeeping, the school's tafsir, the school's hadith, and the opponent's own commentators agree. What remains is the canon the charge calls home.
8. The Christian Canon on the Divine We

The method of the charge, reading a divine plural as plurality of agents, has a home address. It is the method Christians apply to Genesis. The canon that says let us make man in our image also says the LORD our God is one LORD. It says of the man that he has become as one of us (Genesis 3:22). It bids the court go down (Genesis 11:7), and it asks who will go for us (Isaiah 6:8), where the I and the us share one sentence. Both readings, the Trinity's and the majesty's, must carry all of these verses alike.
Verse: Genesis 1:26, Westminster Leningrad Codex, Van Dyck, King James Version
Claim: the plural of creation in the Christian canon
Verse: Deuteronomy 6:4, Westminster Leningrad Codex, Van Dyck, King James Version
Claim: the strictest monotheism in the same canon
Verse: Isaiah 6:8, Westminster Leningrad Codex, Van Dyck, King James Version
Claim: the I and the us share one sentence, the canon's own person-shift

Isaiah's call carries the I and the us in one sentence, the Lord sending and a we commissioning, the canon's own person-shift at the throne. Rashi's court reading carries these verses by naming the addressees, and the court reading is plurality without Trinity, creatures around the throne, which is the Quran's own picture wherever its book names the court. One more line closes the door between the readings. Plurality is not triunity. Even a reading that won every pronoun would still have to build exactly three co-eternal persons of one substance out of the verb's number, and no verb carries that freight.

Augustine reads the Genesis plural as the Son's presence in creation, in On the Trinity I.7.14. His argument is that were the Father alone to have made man without the Son, the plural of Genesis 1:26 would never have been written. The Council of Nicaea in 325 confessed one God the Father Almighty, maker of all things. It confessed one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, God from God, of the same substance as the Father. The synagogue's classic commentary reads the plural another way, as God consulting his heavenly court (Rashi on Genesis 1:26), and that reading is as old as the dispute.

The comparison runs on four named tests. First, what each view asks a believer to accept about God. Second, whether each reading coheres with its own scripture. Third, which reading fits the words themselves. Fourth, which demands less of the text.

On the first test, each reading must square with its own scripture's monotheism, and both books hold the pair, plural forms and strict oneness, without dissolving either. On the second, the Quranic reading is a rule of the language the book speaks, settled by dictionaries, grammars, and usage. The Trinitarian reading of Genesis reads the fourth-century creed back into Hebrew written a millennium before it.

On the third test, the words themselves. Augustine argues from the plural pronouns to plurality of persons, so the number of the pronoun is the load-bearing point, and the Hebrew grammar gives it no such freight. The noun of God stands under singular agreement, and Deuteronomy above shows a plural noun of God standing under one LORD, with nobody reading the morphology as a census. Genesis 1:26's verb is plural in form, like the Arabic nahnu, and English answers that case with its own royal we. The queen says we are, and never we is, one speaker under plural agreement. On the fourth test, the plural of majesty needs no extra persons and no creed to import them, while the Trinitarian reading needs Nicaea to decide what the us means.

The strongest remaining objection is the retinue reading. Read the king's we as executors hidden inside the pronoun, and the divine We becomes Allah with his angels as his retinue. The book names the retinue wherever it acts, and the named retinue are creatures under command, worshippers who descend by permission and salute the Prophet, which is not the plurality the charge wants. The charge needs helpers of the divine act who share the act's rank. The book gives creatures who carry out the act of the One. The grammar of majesty and the naming rule together leave the retinue standing only as what has already been named, creatures under command, with nothing between creature and Creator inside the pronoun.

The sophisticated form of the Christian reading does not rest on the pronoun at all. It reads Genesis through John's prologue, all things made through him, and through Paul's by him all things were created. That reading carries its agent into the Hebrew from outside it, and a Christian holds the agent's book to be inside his canon, so the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That is the honest boundary. The pronoun charge is the popular form, and it is the form answered here. The creedal form rests on the creed, and between the two readings the majesty reading is the one the language itself carries. A method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first, and applied with one standard it convicts neither.
Glossary of Key Terms
nahnu. the Arabic we. When Allah says nahnu, the plural is the Arabic plural of majesty, one exalted speaker, and the book names any creature who shares the act.
iltifat. the turn, a named device of Arabic eloquence in which a speaker shifts grammatical person mid-passage, from speaking about Allah to addressing Him, or from first person to third.
the say-verses. the verses that open with qul, say, where Allah composes the Prophet's exact words to recite, the visible grammar of the relay.
qudsi report. a sacred report in which Allah speaks in the first person, relayed by the Prophet and transmitted through the Imams.
riwa'i. the transmitted reports, the hadith layer, as the school calls it.
the Reminder. al-dhikr, the Quran's own name for itself in Qur'an 15:9.
mufassirun. the Quran commentators.
the wilaya verse. Qur'an 5:55, whose plural verbs the school reads of one man, Ali, giving zakat while bowing.

paragraphs.text: والثاني - انه جرى على تعظيم الذكر في خطاب الواحد بلفظ الجمع لعظم القدر كما يقول ذلك المتكلم ، قال الله تعالى " انا نحن نزلنا الذكر وانا له لحافظون " (1) وقال " ولقد خلقنا الانسان " (2) وما جرى مجراه . وروى النضر بن سمأل قال : سئل الخليل عن قوله " رب ارجعون " ففكر ثم قال : سألتموني عن شئ لا أحسنه ولا أعرف معناه ، والله أعلم ، لأنه جمع ، فاستحسن الناس منه ذلك

“Send me back” has three explanations. First, it uses the plural to show greatness, as Allah says, “We sent down the Reminder,” and, “Have you not seen that Allah sent water down from the sky, then We brought forth?” Second, it means, “Angels of my Lord, send me back.” Third, the plural shows repeated pleading. We are kings, sons of kings. Our rule has kept these people alive for ages.

القول الثاني : أن المراد بهذه الآية محمد ﵇ ، لأنه هو المفصل على الكل ، وإنما قال : * (ورفع بعضهم درجات) * على سبيل التنبيه والرمز كمن فعل فعلا عظيما فيقال له : من فعل هذا فيقول أحدكم أو بعضكم ويريد به نفسه ، ويكون ذلك أفخم من التصريح به ، وسئل الحطيئة عن أشعر الناس ، فذكر زهيراً والنابغة ، ثم قال : ولو شئت لذكرت الثالث أراد نفسه ، ولو قال : ولو شئت لذكرت نفسي لم يبق فيه فخامة

The second view is that this verse means Muhammad, since he is the one favored above all others. It says, “He raised some of them in ranks,” as a hint and an allusion. A person may do something great and be asked, “Who did this?” He may answer, “One of you,” or “Some of you,” while meaning himself. This sounds grander than naming himself directly. Al-Hutay'ah was asked who was the greatest poet. He named Zuhayr and al-Nabighah, then said, “If I wished, I could name the third.” He meant himself. Had he said, “If I wished, I could name myself,” the grandeur would have disappeared.

وأشار بقوله (وقد التفت امرؤ القيس) إلى نوع رابع هو الانتقال من التكلم إلى الخطاب في ليلك واقتصر على هذه الأربعة لأنها أكثر الأنواع وأشهرها ... أما في علم المعاني فباعتبار كونه على خلاف مقتضي الظاهر . وأما في البيان فباعتبار أنه إيراد لمعنى واحد في طرق مختلفة الدلالة عليه جلاء وخلفاء وبهذين الاعتبارين يفيد الكلام حسنا ذاتيا للبلاغة . أما في البديع فمن حيث إن فيه جمعا بين صور متقابلة في معنى واحد فكان من المحسنات المعنوية ... فيكون ليلك التفاتا من التكلم إلى الخطاب

His words, “Imru al-Qays shifted,” point to a fourth type, the change from speaking in the first person to addressing someone directly in “your night.” He mentioned these four because they are the most common and famous types. In the science of meanings, this shift differs from what the situation normally requires. In rhetoric, it expresses one meaning through different ways that make it clearer and more vivid. These two aspects give speech its own beauty and eloquence. In literary embellishment, it joins opposite forms within one meaning, so it is a type of meaningful embellishment. Thus, “your night” shifts from the first person to direct address.

A plural word may mean one person. "The idolaters must not maintain Allah's mosques" means the Sacred Mosque. "Those who call out to you" refers to one man who called, "Muhammad, my praise is beauty and my insult is disgrace." "Let a group of believers witness their punishment" leaves the register of the single one and enters another. In the commentary it can be one, two, or more. "See what the messengers return with" refers to one person, as shown by the words, "Return to them." As for His words to Malik, "Cast both of you into Hell," reports from the People of the House say that Allah addressed the Prophet and the Commander of the Faithful. Al-Mubarrad said this is a dual verb used for emphasis, as if He said, "Cast, cast."

quotes.caption: Manaqib Ibn Shahrashub, in Bihar al-Anwar, v16, p336

paragraphs.text: مناقب ابن شهرآشوب : كان له اثنان وعشرون خاصية : كان أحسن الخلائق : " الذي خلقك فسواك (4) " وأجملهم : " لقد خلقنا الانسان في أحسن تقويم (5) "

ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ

alladhi khalaqaka fa-sawwaka fa'adalak ... laqad khalaqna al-insana fi ahsani taqwim
He created you and shaped you. We created the human being in the finest form.
إِذْ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّى خَٰلِقٌۢ بَشَرًۭا مِّن طِينٍۢ فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُۥ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِى فَقَعُوا۟ لَهُۥ سَٰجِدِينَ

وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ ٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِءَادَمَ فَسَجَدُوٓا۟ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ أَبَىٰ وَٱسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ

When We said to the angels, "Bow down before Adam," they bowed down except Iblis. He refused. And he was of the disbelievers.

Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. You who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace.
وَمَا نَتَنَزَّلُ إِلَّا بِأَمْرِ رَبِّكَ ۖ لَهُۥ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا وَمَا خَلْفَنَا وَمَا بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ ۚ وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّۭا

inna anzalnahu fi laylati al-qadr. wa-ma adraka ma laylatu al-qadr. laylatu al-qadri khayrun min alfi shahr. tanazzalu al-mala'ikatu wa-al-ruhu fiha bi-idhni rabbihim min kulli amr

We sent it down on the Night of Decree. What will make you understand what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend in it by their Lord's permission with every command.
وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ وَنَعْلَمُ مَا تُوَسْوِسُ بِهِۦ نَفْسُهُۥ ۖ وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا ٱلذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ لَحَٰفِظُونَ
inna nahnu nazzalna al-dhikra wa-inna lahu la-hafizun

وَٱلسَّمَآءَ بَنَيْنَٰهَا بِأَيْي۟دٍۢ وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ وَٱلْأَرْضَ فَرَشْنَٰهَا فَنِعْمَ ٱلْمَٰهِدُونَ وَمِن كُلِّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَا زَوْجَيْنِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ فَفِرُّوٓا۟ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ ۖ إِنِّى لَكُم مِّنْهُ نَذِيرٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ وَلَا تَجْعَلُوا۟ مَعَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَٰهًا ءَاخَرَ ۖ إِنِّى لَكُم مِّنْهُ نَذِيرٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ

We built the heaven with strength, and We are surely expanding it. We spread out the earth, and how excellent are We at preparing it. We created every thing in pairs, so that you may remember. Flee to Allah. I am a clear warner to you from Him. Do not set up another god beside Allah. I am a clear warner to you from Him.

( والأرض فرشناها ) ... ( فنعم الماهدون ) نحن إذ فعلنا ذلك للمنافع ومصالح العباد ، لا لجر نفع ، ولا لدفع ضرر

The meaning of “We built the sky with strength” is, We built the sky with power. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Qatadah said this means that We created it and raised it in a fine order. “We are fully able” means that We can create what is greater than it. “We spread out the earth.” “How excellent are We at preparing it.” We did this for the benefit and welfare of people. We did not do it to gain benefit or prevent harm.

quotes.caption: al-Tabrisi, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p329

paragraphs.text: ( وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْناها ) أي بسطناها ومهدناها لمنافع العباد وخلقنا من كل شيء صنفين مثل الليل والنهار ، والأرض والسماء ، والشمس والقمر ، والجن والإنس ، والبر والبحر ، وقيل : الزوجين الذكر والأنثى لكي تعلموا أن خالق هذه الأزواج واحد لا يشبهه أحد

We spread out the earth and prepared it for people's needs. We created everything in pairs, such as night and day, earth and sky, sun and moon, jinn and humans, and land and sea. It is also said that the pair means male and female, so that you may know that the Creator of these pairs is One and that nothing resembles Him.

( بيان ) تشير الآيات إلى عدة من آيات الله الدالة على وحدانيته في الربوبية ورجوع أمر التدبير في الأرض والسماء والناس وأرزاقهم إليه ... والاستنتاج الآتي في آخر هذه الآيات في قوله : ( ففروا إلى الله - إلى أن قال - ولا تجعلوا مع الله إلها آخر ) الآية ، يشهد على أن سوق هذه الآيات والدلائل لاثبات وحدانيته تعالى في الربوبية

Explanation. The verses point to several signs of Allah that prove He alone governs all things. He directs the earth, the sky, people, and their provision. The conclusion at the end says, "Flee to Allah," then, "Do not set up another god with Allah." This shows that these verses and proofs establish that Allah alone rules and governs.

سورة الاخلاص مكية آياتها خمس ط (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم قل هو الله أحد) اي هو الله الأحد وكان سبب نزولها ان اليهود جاءت إلى رسول الله ﵌ فقالت : ما نسب ربك ؟ فأنزل الله (قل هو الله أحد الله الصمد لم يلد ولم يولد ولم يكن له كفوا أحد) ومعنى قوله : أحد أحدي النعت كما قال رسول الله ﵌ : نور لا ظلام فيه وعلم لا جهل فيه وقوله : الصمد ، اي الذي لا مدخل فيه وقوله : لم يلد ، اي لم يحدث ولم يولد ولم يكن له كفوا أحد ، قال : لا له كفو ولا شبيه ولا شريك ولا ظهير ولا معين .

Surat al-Ikhlas was revealed in Mecca. It has five verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Say, 'He is Allah, the One.' The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah and asked, "What is your Lord's lineage?" Then Allah revealed, "Say, He is Allah, the One, Allah, the Everlasting Refuge. He did not beget, and He was not born. No one is equal to Him." Ahad means that His attributes are unique. The Messenger of Allah said, "He is a light free of darkness and knowledge free of ignorance." Al-Samad means the One with no opening within Him. "He did not beget" means that He did not bring anything into existence. "He was not born, and no one is equal to Him." He has no equal, no likeness, no partner, no supporter, and no helper.

وفي إيراد « إياك » دون « إياه » ، كما هو مقتضى الظاهر ، التفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب . ومن النكتة الخاصة ، في الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ، في هذا المقام ، بعد اشتماله على فائدة عامة ، من جهة المتكلم ، وهي التصرف والافتنان في وجود الكلام واظهار القدرة عليها ، ومن جهة المخاطب ، وهي تطرية نشاطه في سماع الكلام ، وايقاظه للإصغاء إليه . أنه لما قيل : « إياك » بدل « إياه » ، فقد نزل الغائب بواسطة أوصافه المذكورة التي أوجب تميزه وانكشافه ، حتى صار كأنه تبدل خفاء غيبته ، بجلاء حضوره ، منزلة المخاطب في التمييز والظهور

The use of iyyaka carries the speech from referring to someone absent into directly addressing Him. This shift has a general benefit. For the speaker, it shows skill and variety in expression. For the hearer, it renews attention and wakes the listener to hear carefully. Here it has a further purpose. The word iyyaka brings the One previously spoken of through His qualities into the position of one directly addressed. Those qualities distinguished Him and made Him known. The hiddenness of His absence became as clear as His presence. He therefore became like one directly addressed in clarity and distinction.
وأعلم أن في الآيات موارد من الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ومن خطاب الجمع إلى خطاب المفرد وبالعكس وفيها موارد من وضع الظاهر موضع الضمير كتكرر لفظ الجلالة في عدة مواضع والنكتة في الجميع ظاهرة للمتأمل

Know that these verses include shifts from speaking about Allah to speaking directly to Him. They also shift between addressing many people and addressing one person. In some places, they use an explicit noun where a pronoun would usually appear, such as repeating the name Allah several times. A thoughtful reader can see the purpose of all these expressions.

quotes.caption: al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v1, p122

paragraphs.text: (فقال : إذا قيل لهم) الضمير للناس في قوله تعالى : (يا أيها الناس كلوا مما في الأرض حلالاً طيباً ولا تتبعوا خطوات الشيطان) على سبيل الالتفات من الخطاب إلى الغيبة للتنبيه على بعدهم عن رتبة الخطاب بسبب سلوكهم طريق التقليد

In the words, "When it is said to them," the pronoun refers to the people in Allah's words, "People, eat what is lawful and good on the earth. Do not follow Satan's footsteps." The speech shifts from directly addressing them to speaking about them. This alerts us that following imitation has kept them far from the rank of direct address.

quotes.caption: al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v3, p204

paragraphs.text: (الذي لا يدركنا الغالي) الموصول صفة للنمط الأوسط وإفراده باعتبار اللّفظ والأصل أن يقول لا يدركه بالضمير للموصول إلاّ أنّه أتى بضمير المتكلّم من باب الالتفات من الغيبة إلى التكلّم للتصريح بالمقصود كما في قول أمير المؤمنين (﵇) : «أنا الّذي سمّتني أمي حيدرة»

In “the extremist cannot grasp us,” the relative pronoun describes the middle pattern. It is singular because of its wording. The original wording would be “cannot grasp him,” using a pronoun that refers back to the relative pronoun. The verse brings the first-person pronoun, a shift from the third person to the first. It states the intended meaning plainly, as Amir al-Muminin said, “I am the one my mother named Haydara.”

ثم التفات من التكلم إلى الغيبة بقوله - واعلموا أنكم غير معجزي الله وأن الله - وأصله واعلموا أنكم غير معجزي وأنى ، وفي هذا الالتفات بعد الالتفات الأول افتنان في أساليب البلاغة وتفخيم للشأن وتعظيم للأمر ... وكل هذا من حسنات الفصاحة

Then the speech turns from "We" to speaking about Allah by name in, "Know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah..." Its original form was, "Know that you cannot escape Me, and that I..." This shift, after the first shift, shows variety in eloquent expression. It gives the matter greater weight and importance. All of this belongs to the beauties of eloquence.
قُلْ مَن كَانَ عَدُوًّۭا لِّجِبْرِيلَ فَإِنَّهُۥ نَزَّلَهُۥ عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ مُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَهُدًۭى وَبُشْرَىٰ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
qul man kana 'aduwwan li-jibrila fa-innahu nazzalahu 'ala qalbika bi-idhni Allahi musaddiqan lima bayna yadayhi wa-hudan wa-bushra lil-mu'minin
Say, whoever is an enemy of Jibril, it was he who brought it down upon your heart by Allah's permission, confirming what was before it, and guidance and good news for the believers.

quotes.caption: al-Tabrisi's gloss, in Bihar al-Anwar, v18, p173

paragraphs.text: وقال في قوله تعالى : " إنه لقول رسول كريم " أي إن القرآن قول رسول كريم على ربه وهو جبرئيل (﵇) ، وهو كلام الله أنزله على لسانه ، ثم وصف جبرئيل فقال : " ذي قوة " أي فيما كلف وامر به من العلم والعمل وتبليغ الرسالة ... " أمين " على وحي الله ورسالاته إلى أنبيائه

Regarding Allah's words, "It is truly the word of a noble messenger," he said that the Quran is the word brought by a noble messenger before his Lord, who is Jibril. It is Allah's speech, which He sent down through Jibril. Allah then describes Jibril, "Possessing strength," meaning strength in the knowledge, actions, and delivery of the message entrusted to him. "Trustworthy," meaning trustworthy with Allah's revelation and His messages to His prophets.

quotes.caption: from al-Hasan, in Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v1, p118

paragraphs.text: روي عن الحسن أن سائلا سأل النبي ( ص ) أقريب ربنا فنناجيه أم بعيد فنناديه ؟ فنزلت الآية
Hasan reported that a questioner asked the Prophet, "Is our Lord near, so we may speak quietly to Him, or far, so we must call out to Him?" Then the verse came down.
وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ ۖ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ ٱلدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ ۖ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا۟ لِى وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا۟ بِى لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ
wa-idha sa'alaka 'ibadi 'anni fa-inni qarib. ujibu da'wata al-da'i idha da'an. fa-l-yastajibu li wa-l-yu'minu bi la'allahum yarshudun
When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me. Let them answer Me and believe in Me, so that they may be rightly guided.

حدثنا محمد بن القاسم المفسر الأسترآبادي ﵁ قال : حدثنا يوسف بن محمد بن زياد وعلي بن محمد بن سيار عن أبويهما عن الحسن بن علي عن أبيه علي بن محمد عن أبيه محمد بن علي عن أبيه الرضا علي بن موسى عن أبيه موسى بن جعفر عن أبيه جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه محمد بن علي عن أبيه علي بن الحسين عن أبيه الحسين بن علي عن أبيه أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب ﵈ قال : قال رسول الله : قال الله ﷿ : قسمت فاتحه الكتاب بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي ولعبدي ما سال إذا قال العبد (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم) قال الله جل جلاله : بدأ عبدي باسمي وحق على أن أتمم له أموره وأبارك له في أحواله فإذا قال : (الحمد لله رب العالمين) قال الله ﷿ : حمدني عبدي وعلم أن النعم التي له من عندي وان البلايا التي دفعت عنه فبطولي أشهدكم انى أضيف له إلى نعم الدنيا نعم الآخرة ... فإذا قال : (إياك نعبد) قال الله ﷿ : صدق عبدي إياي يعبد ... فإذا قال : (اهدنا الصراط المستقيم) إلى آخر السورة قال الله ﷿ : هذا لعبدي ولعبدي ما سال

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, the commentator from Astarabad, reported from Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sayyar, from their fathers, from Hasan ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn Muhammad, from his father Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father al-Rida Ali ibn Musa, from his father Musa ibn Jafar, from his father Jafar ibn Muhammad, from his father Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father al-Husayn ibn Ali, from his father Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib. The Messenger of Allah said that Allah said, "I divided the Opening of the Book between Me and My servant. Half belongs to Me, and half belongs to My servant. My servant will receive what he asks for." When the servant says, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," Allah says, "My servant began with My name. I will complete his affairs and bless his circumstances." When the servant says, "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds," Allah says, "My servant praised Me. He knows that every blessing he has comes from Me, and that I turned away the trials that missed him through My grace. I call you to witness that I will add the blessings of the next life to his blessings in this life." When the servant says, "You alone we worship," Allah says, "My servant has spoken truly. He worships Me alone." When the servant says, "Guide us on the straight path," until the end of the chapter, Allah says, "This belongs to My servant. My servant will receive what he asks for."

علي بن إبراهيم ، عن أبيه ، عن صفوان بن يحيى ، عن إسحاق بن عمار ، عن بعض أصحابه ، عن أبي عبد الله (﵇) قال : إن لله ﷿ ثلاث ساعات في الليل وثلاث ساعات في النهار يمجد فيهن نفسه ... يقول : إني أنا الله رب العالمين ، إني أنا الله العلي العظيم ، إني أنا الله العزيز الحكيم ، إني أنا الله الغفور الرحيم ، إني أنا الله الرحمن الرحيم ، إني أنا الله مالك يوم الدين ، إني أنا الله لم أزل ولا أزال ... إني أنا الله الواحد الصمد ... إني أنا الله الكبير المتعال . قال : ثم قال أبو عبد الله (﵇) من عنده ، والكبرياء رداءه فمن نازعه شيئا من ذلك أكبه الله في النار ، ثم قال : ما من عبد مؤمن يدعو بهن مقبلا قلبه إلى الله ﷿ إلا قضى حاجته

Ali ibn Ibrahim reported from his father, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from one of his companions, that Abu Abd Allah said, "Allah has three hours in the night and three hours in the day when He praises Himself. He says, 'I am Allah, Lord of all worlds. I am Allah, the Most High, the Great. I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. I am Allah, the Forgiving, the Merciful. I am Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I am Allah, Master of the Day of Judgment. I am Allah. I have always existed, and I will always exist. I am Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge. I am Allah, the Great, the Most High.'" Abu Abd Allah continued, "Greatness belongs to Allah, and majesty is His cloak. Allah will throw into the Fire anyone who disputes any part of that with Him. No believing servant calls upon Allah with these words while turning his heart toward Him except that Allah fulfills his need."

محمد بن يحيى ، عن أحمد بن محمد بن عيسى ، عن أحمد بن محمد بن أبي نصر قال : قلت لأبي الحسن (﵇) : جعلت فداك إني قد سألت الله حاجة منذ كذا وكذا سنة وقد دخل قلبي من إبطائها شئ ، فقال : يا أحمد إياك والشيطان أن يكون له عليك سبيل حتى يقنطك ... فكن بالله أوثق فإنك على موعد من الله ، أليس الله ﷿ يقول : " وإذا سألك عبادي عني فإني قريب أجيب دعوة الداع دعان (1) " وقال : " لا تقنطوا من رحمة الله (2) " وقال : " والله يعدكم مغفرة منه وفضلا (3) " فكن بالله ﷿ أوثق منك بغيره

Muhammad ibn Yahya reported from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, who said, "I said to Abu al-Hasan, 'May I be your ransom. I have asked Allah for something for many years, and its delay has troubled my heart.'" Abu al-Hasan replied, "Ahmad, beware of Satan. Do not let him gain power over you and make you lose hope. Trust Allah more deeply. Allah has promised you. Does Allah not say, 'When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me'? He also says, 'Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy.' He says, 'Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty.' Trust Allah more than you trust anyone else."

quotes.caption: Imam al-Sadiq, relaying Ali ibn al-Husayn, al-Kafi, v1, p296

paragraphs.text: وبهذا الاسناد ، عن أبي عبد الله ﵇ قال : كان علي بن الحسين صلوات الله عليه يقول : " إنا أنزلناه في ليلة القدر " صدق الله ﷿ أنزل الله القرآن في ليلة القدر " وما أدراك ما ليلة القدر " قال رسول الله ﵌ : لا أدري ، قال الله ﷿ " ليلة القدر خير من الف شهر " ليس فيها ليلة القدر ، قال لرسول الله ﵌ : وهل تدري لم هي خير من الف شهر ؟ قال لا ، قال : لأنها تنزل فيها الملائكة والروح بإذن ربهم من كل أمر ، وإذا أذن الله ﷿ بشئ فقد رضيه " سلام هي حتى مطلع الفجر " يقول : تسلم عليك يا محمد ملائكتي وروحي بسلامي من أول ما يهبطون إلى مطلع الفجر

Through the same chain, Abu Abd Allah reported that Ali ibn al-Husayn would say, "Allah spoke the truth when He said, 'We sent it down on the Night of Decree.' Allah sent down the Quran on the Night of Decree. 'What will make you know what the Night of Decree is?'" The Messenger of Allah said, "I do not know." Allah said, "The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months." No Night of Decree exists within those thousand months. Allah asked the Messenger of Allah, "Do you know why it is better than a thousand months?" The Messenger of Allah replied, "No." Allah said, "The angels and the Spirit descend in it, by their Lord's permission, with every command. When Allah permits something, He is pleased with it. 'Peace it is until the rising of dawn.' My angels and My Spirit greet you, Muhammad, with My peace from the moment they descend until dawn rises."

الحسين بن محمد ، عن معلى بن محمد ، عمن أخبره ، عن علي بن جعفر قال سمعت أبا الحسن ﵇ يقول : لما رأى رسول الله ﵌ تيما وعديا وبني أمية يركبون منبره أفظعه ، فأنزل الله ﵎ قرآنا يتأسى به : " وإذ قلنا للملائكة اسجدوا لآدم فسجدوا إلا إبليس أبى (5) " ثم أوحى إليه يا محمد إني أمرت فلم اطع فلا تجزع أنت إذا أمرت فلم تطع في وصيك

Husayn ibn Muhammad reported from Mulla ibn Muhammad, from someone who informed him, from Ali ibn Jafar, who said, "I heard Abu al-Hasan say, 'When the Messenger of Allah saw Taym, Adi, and Banu Umayyah climbing his pulpit, it distressed him. Allah sent down Quran to comfort him with, "When We said to the angels, 'Bow down before Adam,' they bowed down, except Iblis. He refused." Then Allah revealed to him, "Muhammad, I commanded and was disobeyed. Do not grieve when you command people regarding your successor and they disobey you."'"

المسألة الرابعة : إذا كان المقصود إثبات التوحيد ، فكيف قال : * ( بنيناها ) * ولم يقل بنيتها أو بناها الله ؟ نقول قوله : * ( بنينا ) * أدل على عدم الشريك في التصرف والاستبداد وقوله بنيتها يمكن أن يكون فيه تشريك ... فإذن علم أن المراد جمع التعظيم وأفاد النص عظمته ، فالعظمة أنفى للشريك فثبت أن قوله : * ( بنيناها ) * أدل على نفي الشريك من بنيتها وبناها الله . فإن قيل : لم قلت : إن الجمع يدل على التعظيم ؟ قلنا الجواب من الوجهين . الأول : أن الكلام على قدر فهم السامع ، والسامع هو الإنسان ، والإنسان يقيس الشاهد على الغائب ، فإن الكبير عندهم من يفعل الشيء بجنده وخدمه ولا يباشر بنفسه ، فيقول الملك فعلنا أي فعله عبادنا بأمرنا ويكون في ذلك تعظيم ، فكذلك في حق الغائب

Fourth question. If the aim is to establish God's oneness, why does He say, "We built it," and not, "I built it," or, "God built it"? We answer, "We built it" more clearly shows that no one shares His control or independent power. "I built it" may suggest a partnership. The intended meaning is therefore the plural of majesty. The wording shows His greatness. His greatness excludes any partner. Thus, "We built it" more clearly denies a partner than "I built it" or "God built it." If someone asks, "Why do you say that the plural shows majesty?" We answer in two ways. First, speech follows what the listener can understand. The listener is human. People compare what they see with what they cannot see. They consider great a ruler who acts through his armies and servants without acting personally. A king says, "We did it," meaning, "Our servants did it by our command." This gives him majesty. The same applies to the Unseen.

quotes.caption: Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, v7, p346

paragraphs.text: والمخصوص بالمدح محذوف تقديره : فلنعم المجيبون نحن ، وجاء بصيغة الجمع للعظمة والكبرياء لقوله : * (فَقَدَرْنَا فَنِعْمَ الْقَادِرُونَ) *

The one praised is omitted. Its meaning is, "How excellent are We in answering." He used the plural form to show majesty and greatness, as in His words, "We determined, and how excellent are We at determining."

والجمع للعظمة والكبرياء وفيه من تعظيم أمر الإجابة ما فيه ؛ وأخرج ابن مردويه عن عائشة رضي اللّه تعالى عنها قالت : «كان النبي صلّى اللّه عليه وسلم إذا صلى في بيتي فمر بهذه الآية وَلَقَدْ نادانا نُوحٌ فَلَنِعْمَ الْمُجِيبُونَ قال : صدقت ربنا أنت أقرب من دعا وأقرب من بغى فنعم المدعو ونعم المعطي ونعم المسؤول ونعم المولى أنت ربنا ونعم النصير»

The plural expresses majesty and greatness, and it gives the act of answering great importance. Ibn Marduyah reported from Aisha that whenever the Prophet prayed in her home and passed this verse, "Noah called upon Us, and how excellent are We in answering," he said, "You have spoken the truth, our Lord. You are nearer than the one who calls upon You, and nearer than the one who transgresses. How excellent are You to call upon, how excellent are You to give, how excellent are You to ask, how excellent are You as Master. You are our Lord, and how excellent are You as Helper."

When the Quranic style says, "I," it points to the oneness of the Divine Being. When it says, "We," it points to the gathering of perfect qualities. Therefore, the pronoun of majesty is necessary. Grammarians say that "We" and "Us" refer to the One who is great. The Truth has declared His own greatness because creating the universe and governing it require a gathering of attributes. Glory be to a Lord beyond every assumption. His majesty is too high for His Being to be fully understood. When He says, "I," that expresses the oneness of His holiness. When He says, "We," that expresses the gathering of His attributes.
